reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: It is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults and may be found incidentally or present with blurred vision, floaters, photopsia, or a visual field defect
Fundus examination classically shows a pigmented dome-shaped or collar-stud (mushroom) mass, often with overlying orange lipofuscin pigment and secondary serous retinal detachment
Amelanotic lesions occur and can be mistaken for other tumours or inflammatory masses
Features that favour melanoma over a benign naevus include thickness greater than about 2 mm, subretinal fluid, orange pigment, symptoms, and proximity to the optic disc
Ultrasound (B-scan) typically shows low internal reflectivity, acoustic hollowing, and choroidal excavation that support the diagnosis
Metastasis is haematogenous and the liver is the dominant site, so systemic staging with liver imaging is essential
Treatment aims to preserve the eye and vision where possible using plaque brachytherapy or proton beam radiotherapy, reserving enucleation for large or advanced tumours
Prognosis relates strongly to tumour size, cell type, extraocular extension, and cytogenetic markers such as monosomy 3
reference.pathophysiology: Choroidal melanoma arises from malignant transformation of melanocytes within the choroidal stroma. Growth breaches Bruch membrane in many tumours, producing the characteristic mushroom shape and disrupting the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and retina, which leads to serous detachment and lipofuscin deposition. Chromosomal changes, notably loss of one copy of chromosome 3 and gains of chromosome 8q, correlate with an aggressive metastatic phenotype. Spread is almost exclusively haematogenous with a strong hepatic tropism, sometimes appearing years after successful local treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Choroidal metastasis from a distant primary
Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
Age-related macular degeneration with haemorrhagic pigment epithelial detachment
additionalInvestigations: B-scan and standardised A-scan ultrasonography to assess dimensions and internal reflectivity
Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and fundus photography to document the lesion and detect risk features
Optical coherence tomography to detect subretinal fluid and confirm dome shape
Systemic staging with liver imaging and liver function tests to detect metastasis
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy for cytogenetic and gene-expression prognostication in selected cases
Fundus autofluorescence to highlight lipofuscin (orange pigment)
redFlags: A malignant intraocular tumour with potential to metastasise, particularly to the liver, requiring urgent oncology referral
Extraocular or optic nerve extension indicating advanced disease
Rapid growth or documented enlargement of a previously stable pigmented lesion
Signs of hepatic metastasis such as deranged liver function or a liver mass
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined mainly by tumour size, cell type, extraocular extension, and cytogenetics; small tumours with disomy 3 have a favourable survival outlook, whereas large tumours with monosomy 3 or chromosome 8q gain carry a high risk of fatal hepatic metastasis, and local eye-preserving radiotherapy controls the tumour without necessarily altering metastatic risk.
pitfalls: Dismissing a small pigmented lesion as a benign naevus without documenting risk features and arranging follow-up
Overlooking an amelanotic melanoma and mistaking it for a benign or inflammatory mass
Failing to arrange systemic staging and long-term surveillance for liver metastasis
Assuming successful local treatment eliminates the risk of later distant spread
management: Treat suitable tumours with eye-preserving radiotherapy — plaque brachytherapy or proton-beam therapy — as the mainstay of local control
Reserve enucleation for large tumours, extensive local invasion or a blind painful eye not amenable to conservative treatment
Consider adjunctive transpupillary thermotherapy or local resection in selected cases
Undertake cytogenetic and gene-expression prognostication for monosomy 3 and chromosome 8q gain on biopsy material to stratify metastatic risk
Stage systemically with liver imaging and maintain lifelong surveillance for the characteristic hepatic metastasis
Refer metastatic disease to medical oncology for options including tebentafusp in HLA-A*02:01-positive patients and liver-directed therapy
Manage through an ocular oncology multidisciplinary team, treating radiation complications such as radiation retinopathy and neovascular glaucoma and providing visual rehabilitation
